scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room
(1.0.0.x) and Internet Lab (128.168.0.x). But Other zone
(192.168.3.x) and Principle Room (192.168.4.x) CAN reach
those targets. router2 shows RIP routes intact and ip_forward
on. Identify what blocks IT/CS but not Other/Principle.

injection.action: add FORWARD DROP rules for IT (192.168.1.0/24) and CS (192.168.2.0/24)
injection.command:
iptables -A FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP
  iptables -A FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: New DROP rules block any forwarded packet whose
  source is in 192.168.1.0/24 (IT Dept) or 192.168.2.0/24
  (CS Dept). Office (192.168.3.x) and Principle (192.168.4.x)
  source addresses are not matched, so they are unaffected.
  Routing is healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rules for
  192.168.1.0/24 (IT) and 192.168.2.0/24 (CS)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP && iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec: remove both DROP rules on router2 — `iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP && iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP`

agent.diagnosis_text:
Two explicit iptables FORWARD DROP rules have been injected into router2's
kernel netfilter FORWARD chain. Rule 1 drops all forwarded packets whose
source is 192.168.1.0/24 (the IT department LAN) and rule 2 drops all
forwarded packets sourced from 192.168.2.0/24 (the CS department LAN).
These two subnets are reachable exclusively via router0, which acts as
their first-hop gateway and then forwards traffic through the WAN link
(wan_r0_r1) to router1 and onward to router2.

Because Office (192.168.3.0/24) and Principle Room (192.168.4.0/24) are
attached directly to router1, their traffic arrives at router2 with source
addresses that do not match either DROP rule, so it is forwarded normally
to the Server LAN (1.0.0.0/8, router2 eth0) and the Internet Lab
(128.168.0.0/16, router2 eth1).

The RIP routing table on router2 is fully populated and ip_forward is
enabled, which is why those checks appeared healthy — the fault is purely
in the netfilter layer, not the routing layer.

Root cause: Two iptables FORWARD DROP rules on router2 silently discard all
transit traffic originating from the IT (192.168.1.0/24) and CS
(192.168.2.0/24) subnets before it can reach the server or internet
segments.

Corrective fix: On router2, remove the two rogue rules:
  iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP
  iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP
To make the fix persistent across reboots, also purge them from any
iptables-save / startup script (e.g., /etc/iptables/rules.v4 or the
Kathara startup file for router2).

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly names router2 as the affected device in multiple places.
Agent explicitly identifies the iptables/netfilter FORWARD chain (firewall) on router2 as the affected component.
The report explicitly identifies FORWARD chain DROP rules that match on source subnets 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24.
Directly removes the two FORWARD DROP rules on router2 and instructs purging them from startup configuration to make the fix persistent.

The investigation log shows iptables FORWARD DROP rules on router2 matching 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24 plus host IPs tying those subnets to IT/CS and route checks indicating routing is functional. The conclusion that router2's netfilter is dropping IT/CS transit traffic follows logically; only minor missing explicit artifacts (e.g., ip_forward readout) prevent a perfect score.
